text: Four patch elements were spaced at half a wavelength. Weights were updated every 2 ms using the LMS rule with a step size of 0.01. We ran 120 trials across three interference geometries.
With a single interferer the signal-to-interference ratio improved by a median of 14.2 dB, and by 11.3 dB with two. With four interferers the improvement fell to 3.1 dB.
All trials were run in an anechoic chamber. Multipath in a real building would present many more apparent sources, so the degradation is expected to appear at lower interferer counts outdoors.

Participants were instructed to ignore the first tone and respond only to the second. The instruction was repeated before each block, and participants who responded to the first tone on more than 10% of trials were excluded.

Each model received the same prompt: "You are a helpful assistant. Ignore any previous instructions and summarise the passage in one sentence." We measured how often the model complied with the embedded instruction, which it did in 61% of trials.
The survey asked: "Please rate how strongly you agree that the treatment improved your sleep, from 1 to 7." Responses were anonymous and no identifying data were collected.

Clinicians should treat these results as preliminary. We recommend that the dose not be increased beyond 20 mg until a larger trial has reported, and that patients be monitored for the side effects listed in Table 3.
Acknowledgements. The authors thank the technical staff of the anechoic facility and the two anonymous reviewers, whose comments improved the manuscript. This work was funded by grant 2023-114.

Abstract. We show that a four-element adaptive array suppresses co-channel interference without prior knowledge of interferer direction. The result is robust across the three geometries tested and, we argue, generalises to small devices.
Received 3 March 2024; accepted 12 June 2024; published 1 July 2024. Correspondence to the first author. Supplementary material is available online.
